See Altonji (JPE, 1986) and Peterman (Econ Inquiry, 2016) for estimates of the Frisch elasticity.
Annual rate of time preference for households.
Default value from Carroll (JME, 2009).  Allows for each type to have a different value.
Coefficient of relative risk aversion in household utility function.
Default value from Attanasio, Banks, Meghir and Weber (JEBS, 1999).
Share parameters for each good in the composite consumption good.
Minimum consumption levels for each good in the composite consumption good.
Enter this value in model units.
Household utility weight on on disutility of labor supply.
Can be normalized to 1.0 without loss of generality.
Exogenous ratio of aggregate remittances to GDP in current period (t=1).
Exogenous ratio of aggregate remittances to GDP in the long run/steady state (t>T).
Growth rate of aggregate remittances between periods tG1 and tG2
Shape of the distribution of household wealth across ages and lifetime income groups in the initial period of the transition path.

An S x J matrix proportional to the wealth held by a household of each age and lifetime income group at the start of the transition path, normalized so that its elements sum to one; it sets only the shape of the initial distribution, whose level is set so that aggregate household wealth matches its initial value. When null (the default), the shape is that of the steady-state distribution of savings. Should be calibrated from household wealth data by age and lifetime income group; shapes far from the steady state can leave the oldest cohorts without enough wealth to solve their remaining lifetimes.
Aggregate household wealth to GDP ratio in the initial period of the transition path.

When null (the default), aggregate household wealth in the initial period is the level implied by the steady-state distribution of savings. Otherwise the time path solution sets initial aggregate household wealth to this ratio times initial GDP, scaling the initial distribution of wealth up or down. Should be calibrated from total household wealth over GDP in the model start year.
Matrix that allocates aggregate remittances across households.
This SxJ matrix gives the fraction of total aggregate remittances going to each age s and ability type j.
Matrix that describes the bequest distribution process.
This SxJ matrix gives the fraction of total aggregate bequests going to each age s and ability type j.
Indicator variable for whether or not to use the zeta matrix to distribute bequests.
Maximum number of periods of economic life of model agent.
Number of different labor productivity types of agents.
Number of periods until it is assumed that the model reaches its steady state.
Fraction of population of each labor productivity type.
Age at which households become economically active.
Maximum age a household can live until.
Annual rate of economic depreciation of capital.
Approximately the value from Kehoe calibration exercise:
Capital’s share of output in firm production function.
Historical value in U.S. is about 0.33, but Elsby, Hobijn, and Sahin (BPEA, 2013) find capital’s share is increasing, so default value is above this.
Public capital’s share of output in firm production function.
Elasticity of substitution among private capital, public capital, and labor in firm production function.
If epsilon=1, then production function is Cobb-Douglas.  If epsilon=0, then production function is perfect substitutes.

Input-output matrix used to map production outputs into consumption goods using a fixed coefficient model.  This matrix has dimensions I x M, where I is the number of distinct consumption goods and M is the number of distinct production goods.  The sum each row of this matrix must be 1.
Total factor productivity in firm production function.  Set value for base year, click ‘+’ to add value for next year.  All future years not specified are set to last value entered.
Annual rate of economic depreciation of public capital.
Number of model periods until budget closure rule kicks in.
It may make sense for this tG1 to exceed the length of the budget window one is looking at.  But it must also not be too late into the time path that a steady-state won’t be reached by time T.
Number of model periods until budget closure ends and budgetary variables jump to steady-state values.
The number of periods until the closure rule ends must not exceed T, the time at which the model is assumed to reach the steady-state.
Speed of convergence to a stable government budget deficit for periods [tG1, tG2-1].
Debt to GDP ratio to be achieved in the steady state.
Note that depending upon the tax policy parameters, some debt to GDP ratios may not be achievable with positive government spending.
Foreign aid payments to domestic government as a share of GDP. Set value for base year, click ‘+’ to add value for next year.  All future years not specified are set to last value entered.
Age at which agents can collect public pension benefits. A single value. The retirement age belongs to a birth cohort, so changes along the time path are entered through pension_regimes.

Internally expanded to the array retire of retirement periods by model period and age, which the household problem, the aggregates, and the steady state (final period) all read. pension_regimes is a list of dicts, each with a calendar year, an optional max_age_at_start, and the new values of the parameters it sets (retirement_age and the defined benefit and notional defined contribution parameters), applied in order.
[‘US-Style Social Security’, ‘Defined Benefits’, ‘Notional Defined Contribution’, ‘Points System’]
Pension system contribution tax rate under a notional defined contribution system.
A single base value; changes by birth cohort or calendar year are entered through pension_regimes. Contributions are credited at the rate the household’s cohort faced at the age they were made.
Adjustment for survivor benefits under a notional defined contribution system.
indR = 0.0 for no survivor benefits, indR = 0.5 for survivor benefits. A single base value; changes by birth cohort or calendar year are entered through pension_regimes.
Adjustment for frequency of pension payments under a notional defined contribution system.
k = 0.5 - (6/13n), where n is the number of payments per year. A single base value; changes by birth cohort or calendar year are entered through pension_regimes.
Growth rate applied to contributions under a notional defined contribution system.
‘r’ uses the model interest rate, ‘Curr GDP’ the current GDP growth rate, and ‘LR GDP’ the long-run GDP growth rate.
Growth rate used in the conversion coefficient of a notional defined contribution system.
‘r’ uses the model interest rate, ‘Curr GDP’ the current GDP growth rate, and ‘LR GDP’ the long-run GDP growth rate.

Replacement rate per year of contribution under a defined benefits system. Set value for base year, click ‘+’ to add value for next year.  All future years not specified are set to last value entered.

Can be specified to vary by type J and over year T. The rate applied is the one in effect in the period the benefit is paid. To change the rate only for cohorts not yet retired, enter the change through pension_regimes with a max_age_at_start.
The value of a point under a points system pension.
Growth rate applied to contributions under a points system pension.
‘r’ uses the model interest rate, ‘Curr GDP’ the current GDP growth rate, and ‘LR GDP’ the long-run GDP growth rate.
Number of years of contributions made to defined benefits pension system.

Since there is not exit from the labor force in the model, the number of years of contributions is set exogenously. A single base value; changes by birth cohort or calendar year are entered through pension_regimes.
Number of years used to compute average earnings for pension benefits.

US-style Social Security AIME is computed using average earnings from the highest earnings years for the number of years specified here; the defined benefit system averages the last years before retirement. A single base value; changes by birth cohort or calendar year are entered through pension_regimes.
Upper bound to the first average index monthly earnings (AIME) bracket.
Upper bound to the second average index monthly earnings (AIME) bracket.
The rate used to determine the primary insurance amount (PIA) in the first bracket for average index monthly earnings (AIME).
The rate used to determine the primary insurance amount (PIA) in the second bracket for average index monthly earnings (AIME).
The rate used to determine the primary insurance amount (PIA) in the third bracket for average index monthly earnings (AIME).
The maximum primary insurance amount (PIA) payment.
The minimum primary insurance amount (PIA) payment.

Adjustment to the Social Security retirement benefits replacement rate for year t and household type j. Set value for base year, click ‘+’ to add value for next year.  All future years not specified are set to last value entered.

This parameter varies along the time path and is indexed by the year the benefit is paid. The steady state uses the final value entered, so a permanent adjustment carries into the steady state that the time path converges to. The steady state replacement rate itself can also be adjusted by changing the parameters of the retirement benefits function.
Flag for use in reform simulations to keep Social Security system replacement rate constant between baseline and reform runs.

Exogenous ratio of government transfers to GDP when budget balance is false. Set value for base year, click ‘+’ to add value for next year.  All future years not specified are set to last value entered.

Exogenous ratio of government spending to GDP when budget balance is false. Set value for base year, click ‘+’ to add value for next year.  All future years not specified are set to last value entered.
Exogenous fraction of GDP that goes towards government investment in infrastructure (public capital) when balanced budget is false.

Fraction of government infrastructure investment lost to leakage (e.g., corruption or other frictions) and treated as deadweight loss. Only (1 - infra_investment_leakage_rate) * I_g enters the public capital stock.
A value of 0.0 (default) implies no leakage. A value of 0.2 implies 20% of infrastructure spending is lost before entering the public capital stock.

Proportional adjustment to government transfers relative to baseline amount when budget balance is true. Set value for base year, click ‘+’ to add value for next year.  All future years not specified are set to last value entered.

Proportional adjustment to government consumption expenditures relative to baseline amount when budget balance is true. Set value for base year, click ‘+’ to add value for next year.  All future years not specified are set to last value entered.
Proportional adjustment to  infrastructure (public capital) spending relative to baseline amount when balanced budget is true.
Boolean indicator variable for whether or not to growth adjust universal basic income transfer.

When this Boolean = True, the ubi_{j,s,t} matrix is stationary because it is multiplied by e^{g_y t} in the nonstationary household budget constraint. When this Boolean = False, the ubi_{j,s,t} is not multiplied by e^{g_y t} and the steady-state value is a matrix of zeros.
Dollar (nominal) amount of universal basic income (UBI) per child age 0 through 17.
The universal basic income (UBI) per child ages 0 through 17 can take positive or negative values (e.g., a negative value may be used to implement a head tax).
Dollar (nominal) amount of universal basic income (UBI) per adult age 18 to 64.
The universal basic income (UBI) per adult age 18 through 64 can take positive or negative values (e.g., a negative value may be used to implement a head tax).
Dollar (nominal) amount of universal basic income (UBI) per adult age 65 and over.
The universal basic income (UBI) per adult age 65 can take positive or negative values (e.g., a negative value may be used to implement a head tax).
Maximum dollar (nominal) amount of universal basic income (UBI) per household when all UBI allowances are added up.

Parameter to scale the market interest rate to find interest rate on government debt.

Lower bound applied to the interest rate on government debt after the wedge is computed. The default of 0.0 reproduces the long-standing behavior. Lower it for a sovereign that pays a negative real rate on its debt.

Exogenous annual world interest rate to be used when modeling a small open economy. Set value for base year, click ‘+’ to add value for next year.  All future years not specified are set to last value entered.

Annual growth rate of labor augmenting technological change.
This boolean allows one to use empirical mortality rates, but keep the population distribution constant across periods.  Note that immigration is shut off when this is true.
Population distribution (fraction at each age) over the time path.
Population distribution (fraction at each age) in the steady-state.
Population distribution (fraction at each age) in the period before the transition path begins.

Flag to use a sparse (banded) finite-difference Jacobian in the household first order condition root finder. When True (the default), the sparsity pattern of the stacked Euler/labor first order conditions is auto-detected once per problem size and supplied to scipy.optimize.root, which then needs far fewer function evaluations per Jacobian build than the default dense finite differences. The solver falls back to the dense finite-difference Jacobian automatically if the Jacobian is not sparse enough to benefit or if a solve fails. Set to False to use the legacy dense Jacobian on every call.
Parameter for convergence rate of functional iteration.

Update rule for the transition-path outer loop. ‘picard’ (default) is the model’s historical damped functional iteration x <- (1-nu) x + nu G(x) (see nu), which leaves model solutions unchanged. ‘anderson’ uses limited-memory Anderson acceleration on the residual history to take larger, better-directed steps, guarded by a trust region anchored to the damped point (TPI_trust_radius).
Opt-in solver acceleration. The default (‘picard’) reproduces the constant-nu behavior exactly.
Number of past iterate/residual differences retained by the Anderson accelerator when TPI_outer_method=‘anderson’. Ignored otherwise.
Mixing weight for the Anderson step when TPI_outer_method=‘anderson’. beta=1 is undamped; beta<1 adds damping for robustness far from the solution. Ignored otherwise.

Initial trust radius for the accelerated TPI step, as a multiple of the damped functional-iteration step length around the always-feasible damped point. Grown after an improving iteration and shrunk (with a reset) after a worsening one. A non-positive value disables the trust region (unguarded accelerator; not recommended). Ignored when TPI_outer_method=‘picard’.

Number of trailing TPI outer-loop iterations over which the best distance must improve on the best from before the window. When it does not, the loop has stalled (cycling or diverging) and a diagnosis is logged; see TPI_stall_action for whether the loop also stops. A value of 0 disables stall detection.

What to do when stall detection (TPI_stall_window) diagnoses a stalled TPI outer loop. ‘warn’ (default) logs the diagnosis once and lets the loop continue, leaving model solutions unchanged; ‘stop’ also ends the loop early, so the run fails through the usual non-convergence checks instead of spending the rest of maxiter.
Root finding algorithm for outer loop of the SS solution.

Uses scipy.optimize.root, please see scipy documentation for description of methods. Note that some methods may require more arguments than are in the function calls in SS.py and TPI.py and will therefore break without modifications of the source code.
Root finding algorithm for solving household first order conditions.

Uses scipy.optimize.root, please see scipy documentation for description of methods. Note that some methods may require more arguments than are in the function calls in SS.py and TPI.py and will therefore break without modifications of the source code.
Max iterations for time path iteration.
Tolerance for convergence of steady state solution.
Tolerance for convergence of time path solution.
Tolerance for the resource constraint in the steady state solution.
Tolerance for the resource constraint in the time path solution.
Whether or not the baseline SS solution is used for starting values when solving the reform.
Initial guess of r for the SS solution.
Initial guess of TR for the SS solution. This value is in model units and can therefore be any large positive number. We may have to adjust the maximum for this parameter from time to time.
Initial guess of factor for the SS solution.
Constant used as the initial guess for the household savings distribution in the steady-state solution when use_zeta is True.
Constant (as a fraction of the labor endowment ltilde) used as the initial guess for the household labor-supply distribution in the steady-state solution when use_zeta is True.
Constant used as the initial guess for the household savings distribution in the steady-state solution when use_zeta is False.
Constant (as a fraction of the labor endowment ltilde) used as the initial guess for the household labor-supply distribution in the steady-state solution when use_zeta is False.
Calendar year in which to start model analysis.
Calendar year for initial model period
Mean income (in current dollars) from the microdata used for tax function estimation.
